About this citation

Three books of essays, and the numbering is by book, so an essay reference without the book is ambiguous. Montaigne revised continually, and the 1595 edition adds material he wrote after 1588 — which means editions differ in what a given essay contains.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to essays on the "civilization of the universal" and files it under Africana Philosophy.

About Léopold Sédar Senghor

Léopold Sédar Senghor (1906–2001) was a Senegalese poet, theorist of Négritude, and Senegal’s first president. With Césaire and Damas he forged a black cultural affirmation in French; his essays treat Négritude as an ontology and aesthetics of vital force as well as a politics of cultural rendezvous.

How to read this passage

Social philosophy asks how individuals and collectives constitute each other, and what justice requires of shared life. This passage enters that discussion through society, humanity.
